extracted.intended_audience: Researchers and institutions applying for NIH/NIAID research project grants (applicants preparing submissions and responding to summary statements)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how NIH/NIAID peer reviewers score research project grant applications, what the core review criteria mean, how overall impact is assigned and calculated, and how applicants should interpret and act on summary statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Your overall impact score is the key review outcome, the main basis for a funding decision by an NIH Institute. NIH defines impact as the likelihood that your project will exert a powerful influence on its field. Reviewers also usually comment on its relevance to the NIH mission: improving human health through science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The overall impact score reflects reviewers' judgment of the extent to which the project can make an impact and is not a mathematical sum or mean of the criterion scores. A raw score of 1 is highest impact and 9 is lowest; reviewers vote with whole numbers 1–9, scores are averaged and rounded to one decimal, then multiplied by 10 to yield the overall impact score (e.g., average 1.34 → 1.3 → overall impact 13). Some applications also receive percentiles (e.g., R01s). Assigned reviewers give preliminary overall impact scores before the meeting; after discussion they may suggest changes; all reviewers then vote. After the meeting, reviewers can edit criterion scores and critiques but cannot change final overall impact scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Significance — the importance of your project: will it advance your field and fit the NIH mission to improve health through science?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Significance is used to assess a project's importance (together with Innovation). It does not take into account your ability to conduct the research. Reviewers may note if success seems unlikely, but that should not affect the Significance criterion score. An application can be judged to have outstanding overall impact primarily because of very high significance even if other criteria are less strong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigator
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigator — assessment of the qualifications of the principal investigator(s) and team to conduct the proposed work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers rely mainly on Biosketches to gauge the Investigator criterion. Investigator, together with Approach and Environment, is used to assess the project's likelihood of success (feasibility). The implicit question: Are the PIs and key personnel well qualified to carry out the project?

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Innovation — assessment of whether the project uses novel concepts, methods, or approaches and will advance the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Innovation, together with Significance, is used to assess a project's importance. Reviewers look for novel concepts or approaches; however, projects with high importance but low innovation can still receive exceptional overall impact scores if they are essential to move a field forward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Approach — assessment of the strategy, methodology, and analyses proposed to accomplish the aims; a key determinant of feasibility and rigor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers read the Research Strategy for detailed information on Approach. Approach is considered (with Investigator and Environment) to assess likelihood of success. Rigor and feasibility considerations, including experimental design and methods, are central to this criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Environment — assessment of institutional support, facilities, and resources that will contribute to the project's success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers typically consult the Resources sections to gauge the Environment. The institutional setting and available resources are used to assess whether the project has the support needed to succeed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and weighting of review criteria in overall impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Review criteria inform but do not strictly determine the overall impact score; reviewers weigh criteria as they see fit and base judgments on their ideal of an outstanding application in the field of science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because overall impact is not a sum/mean, reviewers may prioritize certain criteria depending on the project and field. Examples: highly important research may get an exceptional score despite low innovation; strong synergy among components in multi-component applications (P01, U19) can produce an overall impact greater than the average of component scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with policies for sensitive areas (human subjects, vertebrate animals, biohazards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers check that proposed experiments comply with NIH policies for sensitive areas such as human subjects, vertebrate animals, and biohazards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Noncompliance or concerns in these areas can create 'bars to award' — codes in the summary statement that block funding until resolved. If a summary statement contains such a code, an award cannot be made until the issue is addressed. See specific Human Subjects and Animal Subjects codes for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation and clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: The quality of presentation — writing, cohesion, clarity, absence of typos and internal inconsistencies — influences reviewer judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although reviewers assess the science, poor presentation can harm scores. Cohesive, clear writing and well-organized applications help reviewers understand and favorably evaluate the proposal. Many typos or internal inconsistencies can lead to a lower score.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring process and numerical calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures reviewers follow to assign scores and derive the official overall impact score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assigned reviewers score each criterion and give a preliminary overall impact score before the meeting. During the meeting the assigned reviewers may suggest a different overall impact score; then all reviewers privately mark an overall impact score (1–9). Scores from voting reviewers are averaged and rounded to one decimal place, then multiplied by 10 to yield the overall impact score. After the meeting, reviewers can edit criterion scores and critiques but cannot change final overall impact scores. For some application types (e.g., R01), percentiles are also calculated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary statement content
rubrics_metrics.description: The summary statement provides reviewers' critiques and administrative information following peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical contents include bulleted critiques from assigned reviewers, a brief summary of the discussion, overall impact score and percentile for R01s, criterion scores from assigned reviewers, human and animal subjects codes, any administrative comments, and budget recommendations. Summary statements are uploaded to the Commons within about 30 days, and scores are released in the Commons within 3 business days. The statement is not an exhaustive teaching tool; it contains key critiques but not every problematic point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bars to award and subject/animal codes
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative codes in the summary statement that indicate issues preventing an award until resolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bars reflect the study section's concerns about human subjects, vertebrate animals, or biohazards. If present, an award cannot be made until the issue is resolved; contact your program officer immediately. See the 'Bars to Grant Awards SOP' and the specific Research Animals and Human Subjects codes for meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-review actions and program officer engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommended actions for applicants after receiving the summary statement, including contacting the program officer and planning next steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As soon as you receive your summary statement, check institute paylines and contact your program officer to ask about probability of funding and options if your score is outside the funding range. Ask whether the program officer or a representative attended the review as an observer for additional insight. If you need to revise and resubmit, use the program officer's advice to supplement the summary statement feedback. If funding is likely, review the summary statement to prepare for potential just-in-time (pre-award) requests. If problems are fixable, begin revising quickly because resubmission windows may be short.
